# Equivalence Trials {#sec-equivalence-trials}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Define lower and upper equivalence bounds.
- Explain the logic of two one-sided tests.
:::

## The idea

Equivalence asks whether a treatment difference is sufficiently close to zero that clinically important departures in either direction can be excluded. Set a lower bound $L$ and upper bound $U$ in advance, commonly with $L<0<U$. A two-one-sided-test (TOST) approach requires evidence that $\Delta>L$ **and** $\Delta<U$ at the chosen per-test alpha, which corresponds to an appropriate confidence interval lying entirely within the bounds.

## When and how to apply it

A two-sided test against zero does not answer this question. Nor does calculating power separately for each one-sided component and treating the larger value as joint power. The trial objective and clinically justified margins govern planning.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
For a standardised difference margin of (-0.10,+0.10), compare a confidence interval (-0.08,+0.07) with (-0.12,+0.04). Only the former is wholly inside the interval.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
A nonsignificant equality test is not an equivalence test.
:::

## Key message

Equivalence requires both one-sided criteria; nonsignificance is not enough.
